(a) National Medals.—The medals struck under this Act are national medals for purposes of chapter 51 of title 31, United States Code. 
    (b) Numismatic Items.—For purposes of sections 5134 and 5136 of title 31, United States Code, all medals struck under this Act shall be considered to be numismatic items.

fable.w: This section only classifies medals as national medals and numismatic items for purposes of title 31. A tempting reading is that medal statutes often involve outside advisory boards or designs chosen in consultation with outsiders, but nothing here involves any outside party, consultation, hearing, rulemaking, or right to sue. It is a status provision with no participation process.
fable.s: The medals struck under this Act are national medals for purposes of chapter 51 of title 31, United States Code.

qwen_block.w: This section provides statutory definitions and classifications for medals struck under the Act. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before a federal decision is made. It is purely administrative and definitional.
qwen_block.s:
(a) National Medals.—The medals struck under this Act are national medals for purposes of chapter 51 of title 31, United States Code. 
    (b) Numismatic Items.—For purposes of sections 5134 and 5136 of title 31, United States Code, all medals struck under this Act shall be considered to be numismatic items.

opus.w: The section only says the medals are national medals and numismatic items for purposes of title 31. It does not involve any state, tribe, expert, company, or member of the public in a federal decision. It sets up no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue.
opus.b: The section only classifies the medals: they are "national medals" and "numismatic items" under title 31. The word "national" might suggest a public process, but no outside party is consulted, given a hearing, asked for comments, or allowed to object.

qwen_chat.w: This section merely defines the legal status of medals as 'national medals' and 'numismatic items' for the purpose of applying other sections of the U.S. Code. It does not establish any advisory committee, public hearing, comment period, or consultation requirement involving parties outside the federal government. The text is purely definitional and administrative, containing no mechanism for external participation in decision-making.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the medals are "numismatic items" or "national medals," there is an implicit public interest or distribution process that involves the public. However, the text itself only defines the legal classification of the medals for other statutory purposes (taxation, sale, etc.). It does not describe any process of consultation, hearing, comment period, or advisory board involving non-federal parties. The definition of participation requires active involvement of outsiders in a decision-making process, which is absent here.
